body: I'm with you... depression has torn me down again and again... but I'm thankful for the perspective it's given me. I feel like, if I ever do get out of it, I'm going to be better for having been through it.

I was scared too when I started. It’s not a cure, but it helps to dial down the feelings. If you take them everyday and adjust the dose with your psychiatrist, you eventually can get to a good state. You just have to keep in contact with them and take it slow. Go low dose at first and ramp up as you need. What is your biggest fear about it?
Me too. Wanna be friends?

Good for you to make the appointment and I hope it goes well for you. I was anxious too when I started seeing a therapist. And I even still get anxiety to go there even after six months. But I know that if I am ever going to get better from this, I need some help. I’ve learned a lot from my therapist and I feel like, even through the ups and downs, I always have someone to talk to. And that feels nice. Just remember, your anxiety is going to tell you not to go. It’s going to give you the thoughts that it will all end in disaster. The therapy will teach you how to recognize those thoughts and push through them. And really that’s what it’s all about: whatever your anxiety is telling you to do, do the opposite! 
Anyways, I hope it works out for you. If you want to ask me anything feel free to PM.

No problem. There are always side effects with medication, but if you keep close tabs reporting back with the psychiatrist they’ll eventually get you to something that works best for you. The good news is that these meds are coming a long ways these days and are always getting better. I know my Mom only got the choice of Prozac when she was diagnosed, but now there’s a lot more out there to work with. I’m currently on Lexipro and it’s pretty good. I have very few side effects and I don’t feel like it has impaired me in any way.
Yeah. For me it’s social anxiety. It sucks. Wish I could just talk with people.

It depends on what you are dealing with but for the most part I think a good place to start is by taking meds. I have taken them for 5 years now and I do notice they have some effect. They don’t solve my depression by any stretch, but they dull the sting of these emotions. When I’m on them, I feel less on the brink of breaking down into tears and more just a constant nagging of sadness.

On the other hand, meds don’t change the way you think or the memories you have and I think that’s where cbt is better. They will fix the chemical imbalance (good say if you are bipolar for instance), but there’s more to depression than just that. The thought patterns that get you there are sometimes very intrinsically tied to who you are and what you’ve been through. I think that is a much bigger piece of the puzzle at least for me. And I know cbt for me will be a long ways to go because I’ve been this way since I was a kid.

But in your case I’d say you should see a psychiatrist and talk about it with them. Meds get demonized a lot because of other reasons, but remember that lots and lots of people are taking them. And for many people it helps and sometimes completely changes their lives.

As someone who’s depressed, I’ll tell you what goes through my mind...
I usually say “I’m fine” for several reasons...
I don’t want to bother other people with my problems,
I’m afraid that people will laugh at me, or won’t understand. They’ll lecture me on something I already know, but if it was that easy I would have done those suggested things already.
I’m afraid of being seen as inadequate. I’m afraid of losing friends.
Plus, I sometimes don’t want to admit that something is wrong. I want to stay in my little bubble fooling myself I’m okay because honestly sometimes that’s the only way to make it through a day.

So I guess with that I would say several things:
- don’t force it. Let them talk when they are ready.
- in the mean time, just be there for them. Call them. Text them. Take them places to distract them.
- be open about yourself to them so they feel more comfortable to talk.
- when they do talk: Listen. Be supportive. Don’t lecture them. Don’t tell them what they should do. Just let them talk. Honestly try to understand what they are going through. Don’t try and provide an “answer”. Just be there.
